message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code (Title 8, Chapter 92). Below is an overview of key rights you typically enjoy as a renter: | Category | Typical Tenant Rights | Notes | |----------|-----------------------|-------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent as a security deposit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Landlords cannot keep deposits for unpaid utilities or other charges unless specified in the lease. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, livable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural integrity).
• Must comply with local health and safety codes. | If landlord fails to repair, tenants may withhold rent or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • Tenants may pay for necessary repairs themselves and deduct the cost from rent if the landlord fails to act within a reasonable time. | Must give written notice to landlord first; keep receipts. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot disturb your peaceful use of the property without cause. | Includes unreasonable entry, excessive noise, or harassment. | | **Entry Notice** | • Landlord must provide at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies. | Entry times must be reasonable (typically between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m.). | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for leases longer than one year.
• Certain terms (e.g., subletting, pets) require landlord consent. | Oral agreements can still be enforceable but harder to prove. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much rent can increase, but must honor existing lease terms. | For month‑to‑month rentals, landlords can raise rent with proper notice (usually 30 days). | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow court procedures: serve notice, file complaint, attend hearing.
• Common grounds: nonpayment of rent, violation of lease, or unlawful activity. | Evictions cannot be carried out by force or lock‑out tactics. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Fair Housing Act prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, etc. | Landlords cannot refuse to rent or impose different terms because of protected characteristics. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential services (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise agreed. | Tenants may be responsible for certain utilities per lease agreement. | | **Maintenance Responsibilities** | • Tenants must keep the unit clean and report needed repairs promptly. | Failure to report can affect claims for repair‑and‑deduct. | ### Practical Steps If You Encounter Problems 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of lease, notices, emails, photos of damage, and repair receipts. 2. **Written Notice** – Send a written request to the landlord for any needed repairs or to address violations. 3. **Seek Mediation** – Many cities offer free mediation services for landlord‑tenant disputes. 4. **File a Complaint** – If unresolved, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office or local housing authority. 5. **Legal Action** – As a last resort, file a lawsuit in small claims court (for amounts ≤$20,000) or civil court. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Have you received a written lease? - [ ] Is your security deposit returned within 30 days after moving out? - [ ] Are all essential services (heat, water, electricity) functioning? - [ ] Did the landlord give you 24‑hour notice before entering? - [ ] Have you reported any maintenance issues in writing? If you’re unsure whether a particular situation violates your rights, consider consulting a local attorney or contacting the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR) for guidance.
